pr_title: Fix Log Formatter mutating its arguments.
pr_body:
Log Formatter now creates a new object array and inserts the formatted
parameters there instead of the original array.
Also added a test to verify if the types of the original objects remain
unchanged.

Fix #36165

issue_context.title: ILogger mutates the array of objects to format
comments:
OK I took a quick look and this is a bug that's been there forever. My guess is it doesn't show up because what you're showing isn't typical usage. 

The bug is here https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/e3ffd343ad5bd3a999cb9515f59e6e7a777b2c34/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions/src/LogValuesFormatter.cs#L117-L127. When the logger provider tries to turn the object into a string, it get mutated here.

It should just copy the array before modifying it. We should be aware of the performance implications here though since this is a pretty hot and main code path.

> My guess is it doesn't show up because what you're showing isn't typical usage.

It came up after logging a `formattableString.GetArguments()` which contained a `null` value. That argument was changed and a subsequent query to the database produced an unexpected result. See for instance the [FromSqlInterpolated](https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/blob/daf9cf36ffec8769ab4fa0a123a407fb2fd401bf/src/EFCore.Relational/Extensions/RelationalQueryableExtensions.cs#L134) extension method of `DbSet<T>` which works with `FormattableString` objects.
Anyway, thanks for looking into it!
We hit this using FormattedLogValues class directly, we just copy the array before passing it in. Took a while to track down it was formatting code that was causing changes in our arrays.

@WernerMairl Did you investigate implementing an `IFormatProvider` instead? I think that'd avoid the redundant array allocation and still allow customizing the formatting behavior `IEnumerable`.
Implementing via `ICustomFormatter` might increase the number of `string` allocations by disabling the `ISpanFormattable` optimization.

If you worry about the array allocation, then perhaps `LogValuesFormatter.Format(object[])` can do it lazily when it finds an array element that cannot be used as is, i.e. the value is either `null` or an `IEnumerable` other than `string`. However, it would be best to have some benchmarks before adding such complexity. I don't know what fraction of log calls in real programs have null references among the values. For `IEnumerable` values, I suspect the `string.Join(", ", enumerable.Cast<object>().Select(o => o ?? NullValue))` expression in `LogValuesFormatter.FormatArgument(object)` causes so many allocations that the array does not matter. And if the log level is disabled, then the log entry won't be formatted anyway.

If you take my numbers with a grain of salt (haven't been running BenchmarkDotNet a lot), I did some quick benchmarks with some of the things discussed here, like the lazy init or custom formatter. I couldn't yet get the dotnet/runtime repo to build locally for me, so I have created roughly equivalent code in a small repro project to test different scenarios. I am running each method with two different arrays, 10 items each. One that needs mutating (containing IEnumerables and nulls) and one that would end up with the same value and not mutate the array.

```
BenchmarkDotNet=v0.12.1, OS=Windows 10.0.19042
```

**FormatArgument** is similar to the existing code today, that modifies the array in place (I could not get a reliable benchmark for mutated values since the array would be mutated when BenchmarkDotNet warms up and couldn't get IterationSetup working fully)
**AlwaysNewArray** always creates a new array and then runs FormatArgument on all of them
**NewArrayOnDemand** allocates and copies the array only if the value would be mutated
**ICustomFormatter** is using a custom formatter provided to string.Format so the array doesn't have to be mutated
**ICustomFormatterOnDemand** is using a custom formatter only if a value in the array would mutate, otherwise it will use normal string.Format

From my quick tests, it seems to indicate that creating a new array lazily on demand might be a good tradeoff that wouldn't add too much complexity?

I'll see if I can get the dotnet/runtime repo to build locally for me so I can get some more data to compare them with the real code instead and also run all unit tests so I don't break any functionality as well.. ;).

And if the log level is disabled, then the log entry won't be formatted anyway.

review_comments: Might values be Length == 0? There's no benefit allocating in that case.

No, when the values array is either null or of length 0, the [Log formatter is set to null](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/ff1ea091265968e218664aee72a081965945e18a/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions/src/FormattedLogValues.cs#L32-L53) and in that case, array formatting [is skipped](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/ff1ea091265968e218664aee72a081965945e18a/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions/src/FormattedLogValues.cs#L98-L106).

This does makes the check for a null array redundant, no?

It looks like FormatArgument will often just return the input, and if that's the case for all inputs, there's no benefit allocating an array. Seems like this would be better off lazily creating the new array the first time a formatted argument is a different reference than the input. (That will also implicitly take care of the empty case I mentioned.)

On top of that, it looks like this method has four call sites, three of which always pass in a brand new array, where it doesn't matter if the method modifies it.  Seems like there should be a separate path for that, if this really is hot.
